title: The Gulf’s Postwar Playbook
gist: An FP Live event page framing the post-Iran-war Gulf: Iran struck every GCC state within 48 hours of the war starting, breaking the US security bargain, and the Strait of Hormuz remains closed while Iran negotiates its reopening. Accompanying event blurbs flag a durable oil price shock (unreplenished crude reserves, Houthi pressure on Saudi Red Sea exports) and the rise of chokepoints as the primary instrument of economic warfare.

insights.claim: Iran struck every Gulf Cooperation Council country within 48 hours of the war beginning, invalidating the long-standing assumption that US protection alone secures the Gulf states.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Expect a multi-year step-up in Gulf defense procurement and diversification of security partners away from exclusive US reliance — a tailwind for non-US defense exporters and air/missile-defense suppliers.
insights.quote: In the 48 hours after the war began, Iran had struck every country in the Gulf Cooperation Council, upending a long-standing security bargain they held with the United States.
insights.locator: Iran may be inching closer to a deal

insights.claim: Allison Minor, a former National Security Council director for Arabian Peninsula affairs, argues that relying on the United States alone is no longer a viable security strategy for Gulf states.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Watch for new Gulf security and economic partnerships (Europe, China, regional blocs) that reprice defense, infrastructure and sovereign-fund allocation decisions.
insights.quote: She argues that for countries in the Gulf, relying on the United States alone is no longer an option.
insights.locator: Allison Minor served as a National Security Council director

insights.claim: The war has permanently altered the economic and security calculus of Persian Gulf states, not merely imposed a temporary disruption, according to FP's framing of the postwar period.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Treat Gulf risk premia as structurally higher rather than mean-reverting to pre-war levels.
insights.quote: Iran may be inching closer to a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but for the other countries along the Persian Gulf, the war has permanently changed their economic and security considerations.
insights.locator: Iran may be inching closer to a deal

insights.claim: A Saudi-Emirati thaw and a joint Gulf front on deterrence, engagement and freedom of navigation is the policy prescription being pushed by the same analysts shaping post-war Gulf thinking.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Signs of Riyadh-Abu Dhabi policy convergence would mark a de-escalation signal for Gulf shipping and energy risk.
insights.quote: The Gulf needs a joint front on deterrence, engagement, and freedom of navigation.
insights.locator: A Saudi-Emirati Thaw Can Help Contain Iran

themes.theme: Hormuz closure and the oil shock

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz was shut down and Iran was only 'inching closer' to a deal to reopen it as of early August 2026, keeping the world's most important oil chokepoint offline.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Any credible reopening headline is the single largest downside catalyst for crude; until then tanker rates and Gulf-loading differentials stay dislocated.
insights.quote: With the Strait of Hormuz once again shut down and the Houthis attempting to block Saudi exports through the Red Sea, crude prices seem set to soar.

insights.claim: This oil price rise is described as unlikely to reverse quickly because global crude reservoirs have not been restored, removing the inventory buffer that damped previous shocks.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Low starting inventories mean the price curve can stay backwardated for longer; favors upstream cash flows and hurts refiners and energy-intensive importers.
insights.quote: In addition, global reservoirs of crude haven’t been restored, and China may drop its export curbs.

insights.claim: Houthi attempts to block Saudi exports through the Red Sea are compounding the Hormuz closure, squeezing Saudi Arabia's two main export routes simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Two-route strangulation of Saudi barrels is the tail scenario that dwarfs a single-chokepoint disruption; watch Red Sea war-risk insurance rates as the fast indicator.

insights.claim: Beyond the immediate price spike, the durable question is how countries and companies structurally change behavior — a longer-term adaptation cycle rather than a one-off shock.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Position for multi-year capex in energy security, storage and route redundancy rather than a snapback trade.
insights.quote: Beyond the immediate price shock, how will countries and companies adapt their behavior in the longer term?

insights.claim: Export controls between Washington and Beijing and Houthi disruption of Bab el-Mandeb shipping are two expressions of the same phenomenon: chokepoints deployed as economic weapons.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: A single mental model for pricing both trade-policy and maritime risk: map every supply chain to its narrowest physical or regulatory node.
insights.quote: Both represent the embrace of chokepoints as an economic weapon.
insights.locator: The New Rules of Economic Warfare

insights.claim: Edward Fishman, who deployed these tools inside the US Defense, State and Treasury departments, argues the United States built an economic-warfare playbook that is now being used against it.
insights.speaker: Dana Sherne
insights.so_what: Sanctions and export controls are now a two-way risk for US firms; assume reciprocal chokepoint retaliation is the base case, not the tail.
insights.quote: he argues that the United States built a playbook that is now being used against it.
insights.locator: The New Rules of Economic Warfare
